question: How does real property in Delaware become subject to the Unit Property Act (25 Del. C. Ch. 22), Delaware's older condominium statute?
choice_a: The sole owner, or all owners/lessees, submit the property to the Act by a duly recorded declaration
choice_b: It happens automatically once a building has more than four dwelling units
choice_c: The county planning commission votes to designate the property a condominium regime
choice_d: DNREC issues a unit-property certification after a site inspection
explanation: The Unit Property Act applies only to real property whose owner(s) or lessee(s) submit it to the chapter through a duly recorded declaration; it is not triggered automatically by unit count (A), nor created by a planning commission vote (C) or a DNREC certification (D).
source_note: 25 Del. C. Ch. 22 (Unit Property Act), Subchapter I

question: Under the Unit Property Act, a unit owner's proportionate, undivided interest applies to which part of the property?
choice_a: Only the airspace enclosed by the unit's interior walls
choice_b: The common elements, including the land and portions of the building not included within any unit
choice_c: The declarant's remaining unsold inventory of units
choice_d: Adjoining units owned by other unit owners
explanation: Under the Unit Property Act, each unit carries a proportionate undivided interest in the common elements - the land and the portions of the building outside any individual unit, including structural components and shared facilities. It does not extend to other owners' units (D) or unsold declarant inventory (C), and a unit itself is more than bare airspace (B).
source_note: 25 Del. C. Ch. 22 (Unit Property Act), definitions

question: A Delaware condominium's declaration was recorded in 2004. Which body of law primarily governs that community today?
choice_a: The Delaware Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act (DUCIOA) exclusively, as if created new
choice_b: Federal condominium law, since it predates DUCIOA
choice_c: The older Unit Property Act, with only an enumerated set of DUCIOA sections applying to it
choice_d: No statute governs it; only the recorded declaration controls
explanation: DUCIOA (25 Del. C. Ch. 81) applies fully only to common interest communities created on or after its September 30, 2009 applicability date. Communities created earlier remain governed mainly by the Unit Property Act, though the General Assembly made a specific, enumerated list of DUCIOA sections applicable to them as well.
source_note: 25 Del. C. §81-116 (Applicability to new common interest communities; effective date)

question: Under DUCIOA, by when must a reselling unit owner furnish the buyer with the required resale certificate?
choice_a: Any time before the association's next annual meeting
choice_b: Within 60 days after closing
choice_c: Only if the buyer's lender specifically requests it
choice_d: Not later than the time the purchase contract is signed
explanation: 25 Del. C. §81-409 requires the resale certificate - covering assessments, delinquencies, reserves, financial statements, litigation, and insurance, among other disclosures - to be furnished to the purchaser no later than the time the contract is signed, not left until closing (C) or made contingent on a lender's request (D) or the annual meeting cycle (A).
source_note: 25 Del. C. §81-409 (DUCIOA resale certificate)

question: A DUCIOA resale certificate was not delivered to the buyer until after the purchase contract was already signed. What right does this give the buyer?
choice_a: The right to cancel the contract within 5 calendar days after actually receiving the certificate
choice_b: No right at all; a signed contract is final regardless of the certificate
choice_c: The right to demand a new board election before closing
choice_d: An automatic price reduction equal to any unpaid assessments
explanation: Under §81-409, a purchaser who does not receive the resale certificate before signing may cancel the contract within 5 calendar days after receiving it. The statute does not provide for an automatic price adjustment (D) or a forced board election (B), and the contract is not simply final regardless (A).
source_note: 25 Del. C. §81-409 (DUCIOA resale certificate; cancellation right)

question: Under DUCIOA, deposits collected from purchasers by a declarant/homebuilder during the initial offering of units must be handled how?
choice_a: Deposited directly into the declarant's general operating account
choice_b: Placed in escrow with an attorney, licensed real estate broker, or insured institution until closing, purchaser default, or refund
choice_c: Forwarded immediately to the unit owners' association reserve fund
choice_d: Posted as a surety bond with the Delaware Real Estate Commission
explanation: 25 Del. C. §81-410 requires purchaser deposits collected during the offering period to be held in escrow with an attorney, licensed broker, or insured institution until closing, delivery to the declarant on purchaser default, or refund - not mixed into the declarant's operating funds (B), sent to the association (C), or bonded with the Commission (D).
source_note: 25 Del. C. §81-410 (DUCIOA escrow of deposits)

question: Under Delaware's Landlord-Tenant Code, what is the maximum security deposit a landlord may collect for a lease term of one year or longer?
choice_a: One-and-a-half months' rent
choice_b: Two months' rent
choice_c: One month's rent
choice_d: No statutory cap for licensed rental property
explanation: 25 Del. C. §5514 caps the security deposit at one month's rent for leases of one year or longer, one of the stricter deposit caps among the states. There is no basis for a month-and-a-half (A) or two-month (B) cap, and the statute does impose a limit (C).
source_note: 25 Del. C. §5514 (Security deposit)

question: A Delaware landlord fails to return a departed tenant's security deposit or provide an itemized list of deductions within the statutory period. What is the consequence under §5514(g)?
choice_a: The landlord may still keep a standard 20% cleaning deduction
choice_b: The tenant must sue within 5 days or forfeit any claim
choice_c: The landlord may keep the deposit if the tenant does not object in writing
choice_d: The landlord forfeits the right to withhold any portion of the deposit and must return the full amount
explanation: Under §5514(g), a landlord who misses the 20-day deadline to return the deposit or furnish an itemized statement of damages forfeits the right to withhold any part of it and must refund the full deposit. There is no automatic cleaning-fee carve-out (A), no 5-day suit deadline for the tenant (B), and silence by the tenant does not cure the landlord's default (D).
source_note: 25 Del. C. §5514(g) (Security deposit; landlord's failure to comply)

question: Before a Delaware landlord may terminate a tenancy for nonpayment of rent under §5502, the written notice to the tenant must allow at least how long for the tenant to pay?
choice_a: 5 days
choice_b: 48 hours
choice_c: 3 days
choice_d: 10 days
explanation: 25 Del. C. §5502 requires the landlord's written demand to give the tenant not less than 5 days after the notice was given or sent to pay the overdue rent before the rental agreement may be terminated for nonpayment. Shorter periods of 48 hours (A) or 3 days (B), or a longer 10-day period (C), are not what the statute specifies.
source_note: 25 Del. C. §5502 (Landlord remedies for failure to pay rent)

question: A home sells in Kent County, where the county/municipality has enacted only a 0.5% local realty transfer tax. What is the approximate combined Delaware realty transfer tax rate on this sale?
explanation: Delaware's default state realty transfer tax rate is 3%, reduced to 2.5% only where the local jurisdiction has enacted the full 1.5% local tax. In Kent and Sussex Counties, where the local levy is generally 0.5%, the state rate stays at the full 3%, producing a combined rate of about 3.5% - not the 4% combined rate seen in New Castle County (B), and not 2% or a flat 3% alone (A, D).
source_note: 30 Del. C. Ch. 54 (Realty Transfer Tax)

question: A home sells in New Castle County, where the county has enacted the full 1.5% local realty transfer tax. What is the approximate combined Delaware realty transfer tax rate on this sale?
explanation: Because New Castle County has enacted the full 1.5% local realty transfer tax, the state rate drops from its 3% default to 2.5%, yielding a combined rate of about 4% - one of the higher realty transfer tax burdens among U.S. states. The 3.5% combined rate (A) is characteristic of Kent/Sussex, not New Castle.
source_note: 30 Del. C. Ch. 54 (Realty Transfer Tax)

question: Delaware's first-time homebuyer realty transfer tax reduction, for qualifying transactions on or after August 1, 2017, works how?
choice_a: The entire transaction is exempt from realty transfer tax regardless of price
choice_b: The seller's portion of the tax is eliminated entirely
choice_c: The buyer receives a flat $5,000 credit at closing
choice_d: The buyer's portion of the tax is reduced by ½ percent multiplied by the lesser of the property's value or $400,000
explanation: The first-time homebuyer reduction lowers only the grantee's (buyer's) portion of the realty transfer tax by an amount equal to ½ percent multiplied by the lesser of the property's value or $400,000; it does not zero out the tax entirely (B), does not touch the grantor's share (C), and is not a flat dollar credit (D).
source_note: 30 Del. C. Ch. 54 (Realty Transfer Tax; first-time homebuyer reduction)

question: Absent a contrary agreement between the parties, how is Delaware's realty transfer tax apportioned between grantor and grantee?
choice_a: Apportioned equally between grantor and grantee
choice_b: Entirely borne by the grantor (seller)
choice_c: Entirely borne by the grantee (buyer)
choice_d: Split based on each county's own formula
explanation: Delaware's realty transfer tax statute apportions the tax equally between grantor and grantee unless the parties agree otherwise; it is not, by default, placed entirely on one side (A, C) or governed by an ad hoc county-specific split (D).
source_note: 30 Del. C. Ch. 54 (Realty Transfer Tax)

question: A married couple wants to take title to Delaware real estate in a way that automatically gives the survivor full ownership and shields the property from a judgment against only one spouse individually. Which form of concurrent ownership provides this and is available only to married couples?
choice_a: Joint tenancy with right of survivorship
choice_b: Tenancy by the entirety
choice_c: Tenancy in common
choice_d: Community property
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety, a concurrent ownership form recognized under Delaware common law, is available only to married couples, carries a right of survivorship, and generally protects the property from a creditor of only one spouse. Joint tenancy (A) gives survivorship but is not limited to spouses and lacks the same individual-creditor protection; tenancy in common (B) has no survivorship; Delaware is not a community property state (C).
source_note: Delaware common law of concurrent ownership (tenancy by the entirety)

question: A licensee is listing a parcel of unimproved Delaware land that has no connection to public sewer or public water. What is the licensee's disclosure obligation regarding sewer and water?
choice_a: None - disclosure requirements apply only to improved property
choice_b: The licensee must personally conduct a percolation test before listing the property
choice_c: The licensee must provide the buyer with the required Notice to Buyer Regarding Sewer and Water
choice_d: Disclosure may be deferred until the day of closing
explanation: Delaware practice requires licensees selling unimproved land not served by public sewer or water to give the buyer the specific Notice to Buyer Regarding Sewer and Water so the buyer understands that private well/septic arrangements (and any related permitting) will be needed. This obligation is not limited to improved property (A), does not require the agent to personally test soil (B - that is DNREC's site-evaluation role), and is not properly deferred to closing (D).
source_note: Delaware Real Estate Commission disclosure practice for unimproved land

question: Delaware's Fair Housing Act (6 Del. C. Ch. 46) prohibits housing discrimination based on protected characteristics that go beyond the federal Fair Housing Act by also including which of the following?
choice_a: Political party affiliation
choice_b: Homeownership status only
choice_c: Only race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability
choice_d: Source of income, sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, age, creed, and military status
explanation: Delaware's Fair Housing Act expands on the federal law's seven protected classes by also prohibiting discrimination based on source of income, sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, age, creed, and military/housing status. Option D lists only the federal classes without the state additions, and political party affiliation (A) and homeownership status alone (C) are not the additional protections at issue.
source_note: 6 Del. C. Ch. 46 (Delaware Fair Housing Act)

question: Complaints alleging housing discrimination under Delaware's Fair Housing Act are primarily filed with and investigated by which body?
choice_a: The Division of Human and Civil Rights (under the Delaware Human and Civil Rights Commission)
choice_b: The Delaware Real Estate Commission
choice_c: DNREC
choice_d: The county Board of Realtors
explanation: The Delaware Human and Civil Rights Commission implements the Fair Housing Act, with the Division of Human and Civil Rights handling complaint intake, investigation, and conciliation, and the Attorney General available for pattern-or-practice and judicial enforcement. The Real Estate Commission (A) handles licensee discipline, not fair housing complaints generally, and DNREC (B) and local Realtor boards (D) have no role here.
source_note: 6 Del. C. Ch. 46 (Delaware Fair Housing Act; enforcement)

question: A rural Sussex County lot has no access to public sewer and the seller plans to install an individual septic system. Before DNREC will approve a permit for that on-site wastewater system, what must generally occur first?
choice_a: Approval by the buyer's future homeowners' association
choice_b: A site evaluation of the soil to determine its suitability for the proposed wastewater system
choice_c: Nothing; septic permits are issued automatically upon application
choice_d: A signed waiver from every adjoining property owner
explanation: DNREC requires a site evaluation (soil and site suitability testing) as a prerequisite to permitting an on-site wastewater (septic) system on land not served by public sewer. Permits are not automatic (C), and neither an HOA's approval (B) nor adjoining-owner waivers (D) substitute for that DNREC site evaluation.
source_note: DNREC Division of Water, on-site wastewater (septic) permitting program

question: Within DNREC, on-site wastewater (septic) permitting for properties not served by public sewer is administered by which division?
choice_a: Division of Fish and Wildlife
choice_b: Division of Air Quality
choice_c: Division of Water
choice_d: Division of Waste and Hazardous Substances
explanation: DNREC's Division of Water administers the on-site wastewater/septic system program, including site evaluations and permitting for lots without public sewer access. The other listed divisions (A, B, C) handle unrelated environmental programs.
source_note: DNREC Division of Water, on-site wastewater (septic) program

question: Under Delaware's Clear Zone Safety Law (17 Del. C. §525), a real estate "For Sale" sign generally may NOT be placed:
choice_a: On private property with the owner's written consent
choice_b: More than 10 feet from the edge of pavement
choice_c: Anywhere within Kent County
choice_d: Within the first 10 feet of unpaved right-of-way from the edge of pavement (the clear zone)
explanation: The Clear Zone Safety Law bars signs from the clear zone - the first 10 feet of unpaved right-of-way measured from the edge of pavement - along state-maintained roads, for safety reasons. Placement on private property with consent (A) is not itself a right-of-way violation, the restriction is not simply "more than 10 feet away" (B), and the law is not limited to Kent County (D).
source_note: 17 Del. C. §525 (Maintenance of clear zones within rights-of-way); DelDOT roadside control program

question: DelDOT allows a narrow, time-limited exception permitting signs to be placed within the state right-of-way (but still outside the 10-foot clear zone) during a defined window before and after an election. This limited exception applies to:
choice_a: Political/campaign signs only, during the election-season window
choice_b: Any commercial sign under 2 square feet in size
choice_c: Real estate "for sale" and "open house" signs at any time
choice_d: Any sign displayed for fewer than 24 hours
explanation: DelDOT's limited right-of-way exception is specific to political/campaign signage during the roughly 30-day windows before and after an approved election; real estate signs receive no comparable exception and remain barred from the right-of-way and clear zone at all times (C).
source_note: DelDOT Roadside Control & Outdoor Advertising program (sign law FAQ)

question: A real estate sign is found improperly placed within the state right-of-way in violation of Delaware's sign law. What is the general consequence?
choice_a: Automatic revocation of the listing agent's real estate license
choice_b: The sign is removed, and the owner may face a violation fine plus a fee to reclaim the sign
choice_c: No penalty; the state simply relocates the sign for the owner
choice_d: A criminal misdemeanor charge is filed with no removal
explanation: Signs improperly placed in the right-of-way are subject to removal, along with a monetary violation fine and a separate fee to release/reclaim the removed sign - not license revocation (A), a costless relocation service (B), or a criminal-only response with no removal (D).
source_note: DelDOT Roadside Control & Outdoor Advertising program (sign law FAQ)

question: A Delaware seller extends purchase-money financing to the buyer as part of the sale, taking back a mortgage secured by the very property sold. Under Delaware's recording statute, what determines that mortgage's priority against a later lien on the same property?
choice_a: Purchase money mortgages automatically receive first priority under Delaware law regardless of recording
choice_b: Whichever party can show actual knowledge of the other's interest
choice_c: The order in which the instruments are recorded, not the date they were signed
choice_d: A court must decide priority case by case; there is no statutory rule
explanation: 25 Del. C. §153 gives a recorded deed or mortgage priority from the time it is recorded, without regard to when it was signed, sealed, and delivered - a pure recording (race) rule. Delaware law does not grant purchase money mortgages automatic super-priority (A), turn on actual notice (C), or leave priority to ad hoc judicial determination (D).
source_note: 25 Del. C. §153 (Recording; priority)

question: In a Delaware seller-financed transaction, a purchase money mortgage is best described as:
choice_a: A government-subsidized loan program administered by the Delaware State Housing Authority
choice_b: An unsecured personal loan from the seller to the buyer
choice_c: A third-party lender's loan secured by property the buyer already owns
choice_d: Financing extended by the seller to the buyer, secured by a mortgage on the very property being sold
explanation: A purchase money mortgage in a seller-financed sale is financing the seller provides to the buyer, secured by a mortgage lien on the property being conveyed in that same transaction - not an unsecured loan (B), a third-party lender product (C), or a DSHA program (A).
source_note: Delaware conveyancing practice; purchase money mortgage financing

question: A "tax ditch" under Delaware's drainage law (7 Del. C. Ch. 41) is best described as:
choice_a: A drainage improvement organized under a Board of Ditch Commissioners and funded by assessments on benefited landowners
choice_b: A federal flood-insurance zone designation
choice_c: An informal term for a county property tax lien
choice_d: A municipal stormwater sewer connection fee
explanation: Delaware's tax ditch law establishes drainage systems for rural land managed by a Board of Ditch Commissioners, with maintenance and improvement costs funded through assessments on the landowners who benefit from the ditch - it is not a federal flood-zone designation (A), a generic tax lien (B), or a municipal stormwater fee (D).
source_note: 7 Del. C. Ch. 41 (Drainage of Lands and Management of Waters; Tax Ditches)

question: Why should a broker listing rural Delaware land check whether the parcel lies within an organized tax ditch district?
choice_a: Because tax ditch membership automatically exempts the parcel from county property tax
choice_b: Because the parcel may carry ongoing ditch maintenance assessments that run with the land and pass to the new owner
choice_c: Because it has no legal or financial effect on the property
choice_d: Because it automatically rezones the parcel to agricultural use
explanation: Land within a tax ditch district is subject to ongoing assessments to fund the ditch's maintenance and improvement, and that obligation runs with the land to successive owners - it does not exempt the parcel from ordinary property tax (B), does not rezone it (D), and is not simply irrelevant to the property (C).
source_note: 7 Del. C. Ch. 41 (Tax Ditches)

question: Under Delaware's manufactured home community right of first offer (25 Del. C. Ch. 70, Subchapter IV), when a community owner decides to sell, notice of that decision must be given to the homeowners' association and which other parties?
choice_a: No one else; notice to the association alone is sufficient
choice_b: Only the individual resident whose home is closest to the community entrance
choice_c: The Delaware Manufactured Home Owners Association (DMHOA) and the Delaware Manufactured Home Relocation Authority
choice_d: The county register of wills
explanation: The right-of-first-offer notice must go to the resident homeowners' association, the Delaware Manufactured Home Owners Association (DMHOA), and the Delaware Manufactured Home Relocation Authority - not just the association alone (A), a single resident (C), or the register of wills (D).
source_note: 25 Del. C. Ch. 70, Subch. IV (Right of First Offer)

question: Once a Delaware manufactured home community's homeowners' association receives a right-of-first-offer notice of sale, how long does it generally have to respond in writing?
choice_a: 10 calendar days
choice_b: 90 calendar days
choice_c: 60 calendar days
choice_d: 30 calendar days
explanation: The association has 30 calendar days from the date the right-of-first-offer notice is mailed to respond in writing, indicating whether it accepts the offered price, proposes an alternative, or declines to purchase. The statute does not use a 10-day (A), 60-day (C), or 90-day (B) window.
source_note: 25 Del. C. Ch. 70, Subch. IV (Right of First Offer)

question: A manufactured home community's homeowners' association declines to purchase after receiving a right-of-first-offer notice. What must the community owner do before selling to a third party?
choice_a: File an affidavit of compliance, after which the owner may sell freely to a third party
choice_b: Reduce the sale price by a statutorily fixed percentage
choice_c: Obtain court approval for the sale
choice_d: Wait an additional full year regardless of the association's response
explanation: Once the association declines or fails to timely respond, the community owner files an affidavit of compliance and is then free to sell to a third party, with the right-of-first-offer obligation not reviving for the remainder of that 12-month period. There is no court-approval step (B), no fixed price cut (A), and no automatic further year-long delay once compliance is filed (C).
source_note: 25 Del. C. Ch. 70, Subch. IV (Right of First Offer)

question: Under Delaware's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (6 Del. C. Ch. 12A), an electronic signature on a real estate purchase agreement is:
choice_a: Automatically invalid because real property contracts are excluded from UETA
choice_b: Not to be denied legal effect solely because it is electronic, but only as to parties who have agreed to conduct that transaction by electronic means
choice_c: Valid, but only after the document has also been separately notarized
choice_d: Valid regardless of whether the other party ever agreed to transact electronically
explanation: UETA provides that a record or signature may not be denied legal effect or enforceability solely because it is electronic, but it applies only between parties who have each agreed to conduct the transaction electronically - real estate contracts are not on UETA's exclusions list (A), and separate notarization is not a blanket requirement for e-signature validity (B); agreement to transact electronically is required, so (D) is incorrect.
source_note: 6 Del. C. §§ 12A-103, 12A-105, 12A-107 (Delaware UETA)

question: Which document is expressly excluded from Delaware's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, meaning it generally cannot be executed by electronic signature under that Act?
choice_a: A residential purchase and sale agreement
choice_b: A property management agreement
choice_c: A will or codicil
choice_d: A listing agreement between broker and seller
explanation: 6 Del. C. §12A-103 expressly excludes laws governing the creation and execution of wills and codicils from UETA's scope. Purchase agreements (A), property management agreements (B), and listing agreements (C) are not on that exclusions list and are generally within UETA's coverage.
source_note: 6 Del. C. §12A-103 (UETA; scope and exclusions)

question: A nonresident of Delaware sells Delaware real estate. Under 30 Del. C. §1126, how is the estimated Delaware income tax on the sale generally handled?
choice_a: It is deferred until the seller files the following year's federal return
choice_b: It is paid directly to the IRS within 90 days of closing
choice_c: It only applies if the sale proceeds exceed $1 million
choice_d: It is filed and remitted with the deed to the Recorder of Deeds, and the amount due is withheld from the net sale proceeds before the deed may be recorded
explanation: Under 30 Del. C. §1126, a nonresident seller must file the required estimated tax documentation (Form 5403) with the Recorder, remitted along with the deed, and the estimated tax is withheld from the net proceeds of sale before the deed can be recorded. It is not deferred to the following year (A), not paid to the IRS (C - this is a Delaware, not federal, obligation), and not conditioned on a $1 million threshold (D).
source_note: 30 Del. C. §1126 (Withholding of income tax on sale of real estate by nonresidents)

question: Under 30 Del. C. §1126, a nonresident seller may avoid Delaware's standard estimated-tax withholding at closing by instead filing an alternative declaration in which of these circumstances?
choice_a: The transaction qualifies for a capital gain exemption/exclusion, or involves a foreclosure or deed in lieu of foreclosure
choice_b: Whenever the buyer requests it in writing
choice_c: Whenever the sale involves a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: Never; withholding under §1126 is mandatory in every nonresident sale with no exceptions
explanation: §1126 permits a nonresident seller to file an alternative declaration claiming exemption from the standard withholding where the gain qualifies for exclusion, or where the transaction is a foreclosure or deed in lieu of foreclosure. Buyer requests (A) or broker involvement (B) are not the statutory basis for the exemption, and the statute does provide these exceptions, so (D) is incorrect.
source_note: 30 Del. C. §1126(b) (Withholding exemptions)

question: Delaware's Consumer Fraud Act (6 Del. C. Ch. 25, Subch. II) prohibits which conduct in connection with the sale of merchandise, a term broad enough to include real estate and real estate services?
choice_a: Only conduct that also independently violates federal law
choice_b: Deception, fraud, false pretense, false promise, misrepresentation, or the concealment, suppression, or omission of a material fact
choice_c: Only written misrepresentations in contracts exceeding $500
choice_d: Only conduct committed by sellers located outside Delaware
explanation: The Consumer Fraud Act broadly bars deception, fraud, false pretense, false promise, misrepresentation, and the concealment, suppression, or omission of a material fact in connection with the sale of merchandise (which includes real estate and related services). It is not limited to contracts over $500 (C), out-of-state sellers (D), or conduct that also violates federal law (B).
source_note: 6 Del. C. Ch. 25, Subch. II (Consumer Fraud Act)

question: Who enforces Delaware's Consumer Fraud Act, and what is a possible civil penalty for a willful violation?
choice_a: The Real Estate Commission; a maximum $500 fine
choice_b: DNREC; criminal fines only, with no civil remedy available
choice_c: The Attorney General; a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per willful violation
choice_d: Private licensees, resolved only through mandatory arbitration
explanation: The Attorney General enforces the Consumer Fraud Act, with authority to seek injunctions, restitution, and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per willful violation, along with investigative demands and asset-freeze powers. Enforcement is not vested in the Real Estate Commission (A) or DNREC (C), and it is not confined to private arbitration (D).
source_note: 6 Del. C. Ch. 25, Subch. II (Consumer Fraud Act; enforcement and penalties)

question: Performing home inspections for compensation in Delaware requires a license issued and regulated under which authority?
choice_a: The Delaware Real Estate Commission, as an add-on to an existing broker's license
choice_b: No license is required; home inspection is unregulated in Delaware
choice_c: A federal HUD inspector certification
choice_d: 24 Del. C. Ch. 41 (Home Inspectors), regulated by the Board of Home Inspectors
explanation: Delaware licenses and regulates home inspectors under Title 24, Chapter 41, administered by the Board of Home Inspectors - a separate licensing scheme from real estate brokerage (A), not a HUD federal credential (D), and not an unregulated activity (C).
source_note: 24 Del. C. Ch. 41 (Home Inspectors)

question: Under 24 Del. C. §4108, which of the following is a requirement to become a licensed Delaware home inspector?
choice_a: Passing a Board-designated written standardized examination and maintaining professional liability/errors-and-omissions insurance
choice_b: A four-year engineering degree
choice_c: At least 10 years' prior experience as a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: Sponsorship by a licensed general contractor
explanation: §4108 requires applicants to pass a written, standardized examination designated by the Board, complete Board-established training/education, and maintain professional liability and errors-and-omissions insurance, among other requirements - it does not require an engineering degree (A), broker experience (B), or contractor sponsorship (C).
source_note: 24 Del. C. §4108 (Home Inspectors; license qualifications)

question: An individual was actively performing home inspections in Delaware before the licensing law's requirements took effect. Under the statute's grandfather provision, that individual could qualify for licensure without the exam/education requirements by documenting which of the following as of August 6, 2013?
choice_a: A real estate broker's license held for at least one year
choice_b: At least 250 fee-paid Delaware home inspections, or 5 or more years of practice experience
choice_c: Membership in a single national home inspector trade association
choice_d: A written recommendation letter from one past client
explanation: Delaware's grandfather provision allowed inspectors already practicing as of August 6, 2013 to qualify without the exam/education requirements by documenting either 250 or more fee-paid Delaware inspections or 5 or more years of practice experience - not simply a broker's license (A), trade-association membership (C), or a single reference letter (D).
source_note: 24 Del. C. Ch. 41 (Home Inspectors; grandfather provision)

question: Under 25 Del. C. §318, a recorded HOA covenant that effectively prohibits a homeowner from installing a roof-mounted solar energy system is:
choice_a: Fully enforceable if it was recorded before the home was built
choice_b: Enforceable only in communities created before DUCIOA's 2009 applicability date
choice_c: Void and unenforceable, though reasonable restrictions that don't significantly raise cost or reduce system efficiency are still permitted
choice_d: Enforceable if the HOA board unanimously votes to retain it
explanation: §318 voids and makes unenforceable any covenant or restriction that effectively prohibits or unreasonably restricts a roof-mounted solar energy system, while still allowing reasonable restrictions that don't significantly increase cost or decrease the system's efficiency or performance. Recording date (A), a board's unanimous vote (D), and DUCIOA's applicability date (B) do not save a prohibited covenant.
source_note: 25 Del. C. §318 (Restrictive covenants; solar energy devices)

question: Under 25 Del. C. §318, before installing a solar energy system, what notice must a Delaware homeowner generally give?
choice_a: Public notice in a newspaper of general circulation
choice_b: A DNREC environmental impact permit application
choice_c: Sign-off from the county planning commission
choice_d: Notice to the HOA and to neighboring owners within 150 feet, at least 60 days before installation
explanation: §318 requires the property owner to notify the homeowners' association and neighboring owners within 150 feet at least 60 days before installing the system; it does not require newspaper publication (A), a DNREC environmental permit (C), or county planning commission approval (D). The statute also allows an existing restriction on ground-mounted systems to be amended by majority vote of the property owners, unlike the roof-mounted protection, which cannot be overridden by a covenant at all.
source_note: 25 Del. C. §318 (Solar energy devices; notice requirement)
